stills.heading: Harmonic Material and Chord Connections
stills.caption: Lesson 8 · Harmony Course · Storm Studios Learning
stills.narration: Hello, and welcome back to Storm Studios Learning. In lesson six we learned how to build chords for the vocal quartet. In lesson seven we saw how each voice moves, and what to watch for when two voices move at the same time.

stills.heading: Connecting two chords
stills.caption: The last step before the first chorale
stills.narration: Today we will bring both things together: we are going to connect two chords. It is the last step before writing our first chorale.

stills.heading: Three parts
stills.caption: Harmonic material · general table of connections · connection technique
stills.narration: This lesson has three parts: the harmonic material, the general table of connections, and the technique for connecting chords.

stills.heading: Harmonic material
stills.narration: Let's begin with the harmonic material.

stills.heading: The chords we use, and in which position
stills.caption: Bach chorales · triads · major mode
stills.narration: We call harmonic material the chords we use, and the position in which we use them. We follow Bach's chorales, and for now we work only with triads in the major mode.

stills.heading: First degree
stills.caption: Root position and six three
stills.narration: The first degree is used in root position and in first inversion, that is, six three.

stills.heading: Second degree
stills.caption: Root position and six three
stills.narration: The second degree, also in root position and in six three.

stills.heading: Third degree
stills.caption: Root position only
stills.narration: The third degree is used only in root position.

stills.heading: Fourth and fifth degrees
stills.caption: Root position and six three
stills.narration: The fourth and fifth degrees are used in root position and in six three.

stills.heading: Sixth degree
stills.caption: Root position only
stills.narration: The sixth degree, only in root position.

stills.heading: Seventh degree
stills.caption: Six three only
stills.narration: And the seventh degree, only in six three.

stills.heading: Three things about this list
stills.narration: There are three things worth understanding about this list.

stills.heading: No free six four
stills.caption: A fourth forms above the bass · we will see it in specific cases
stills.narration: First, no chord is used freely in second inversion, six four. In six four, a fourth forms above the bass, and that fourth sounds like a dissonance. We will see six four chords later, in specific cases.

stills.heading: III and VI in root position
stills.caption: Two tonal regions · modal color
stills.narration: Second, the third and sixth degrees are used in root position. These chords belong to two tonal regions and have a modal color, and root position gives them stability.

stills.heading: VII only in six three
stills.caption: No diminished fifth above the bass
stills.narration: Third, the seventh degree is a diminished chord, so it is used only in six three. That way we avoid a diminished fifth above the bass.

stills.heading: General table of connections
stills.caption: (6/3): root position or six three
stills.narration: Now let's look at the general table of connections. At least in the classical period, each chord has preferred paths toward other chords. The table tells us which chords each one can go to. When we say a chord is in root position or six three, either position is valid.

stills.heading: From the first degree
stills.caption: I → III must continue to IV
stills.narration: Let's start with the first degree. From the first degree we can go to the second, the third, the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, and the seventh in six three. But be careful: if we go from the first to the third, the third must then go to the fourth.

stills.heading: From the second degree
stills.caption: II → IV must continue to V
stills.narration: From the second degree we can go to the fifth, the seventh in six three, or the fourth. And if we go from the second to the fourth, the fourth must then go to the fifth.

stills.heading: From the third degree
stills.caption: III → V must continue to VI
stills.narration: From the third degree we can go to the fourth, the fifth, the sixth, or the seventh in six three. If we go from the third to the fifth, the fifth must then go to the sixth.

stills.heading: From the fourth degree
stills.narration: From the fourth degree we can go to the first, the second, the fifth, or the seventh in six three.

stills.heading: From the fifth degree
stills.caption: V → VII 6/3 must continue to I
stills.narration: From the fifth degree we can go to the first, the sixth, or the seventh in six three. If we go from the fifth to the seventh, the seventh must then go to the first.

stills.heading: Special case
stills.caption: V in root position → IV 6/3
stills.narration: And there is a special case: the fifth in root position can also go to the fourth in six three.

stills.heading: From the sixth degree
stills.caption: VI → I must continue to II
stills.narration: From the sixth degree we can go almost anywhere: to the first, the second, the third, the fourth, the fifth, and the seventh in six three. If we go from the sixth to the first, the first must then go to the second.

stills.heading: From the seventh degree in six three
stills.narration: And from the seventh degree in six three we can go to the first, the third, the sixth, or the fifth.

stills.heading: Required continuations
stills.caption: They are not suggestions: they are rules
stills.narration: These required continuations are important. When the table says that after a connection we must go on to a certain chord, it is not a suggestion: it is a rule.

stills.heading: Repeating the chord
stills.caption: No connection technique: the voices move freely
stills.narration: One more detail: when we repeat the same chord, there is no connection technique. The voices can move freely within the chord, for example from the first degree to the first degree in six three.

stills.heading: How two chords are connected
stills.narration: Now let's see how two chords are connected.

stills.heading: First, each chord well built
stills.caption: As in lesson 6
stills.narration: First we build each chord as in lesson six. We respect the ranges and the maximum spacing between voices. We use only the notes of the chord, always include the third, never double the leading tone, and the seventh degree is always complete.

stills.heading: Then, each voice
stills.caption: Only allowed melodic intervals
stills.narration: Then we check how each voice moves, as in lesson seven. Each voice uses only the allowed melodic intervals.

stills.heading: The common tone
stills.caption: It stays in the same voice · the others take the shortest path
stills.narration: But now there is something new: a voice may stay on the same note. When two chords share a note, we call it a common tone. It is often best to keep the common tone in the same voice, and move the other voices by the shortest path.

stills.heading: The six pairs of voices
stills.caption: S–A · S–T · S–B · A–T · A–B · T–B
stills.narration: Then we check the six pairs of voices. Soprano and alto, soprano and tenor, soprano and bass, alto and tenor, alto and bass, and tenor and bass.

stills.heading: No parallel or contrary fifths or octaves
stills.caption: Contrary is fine outside soprano and bass · no simultaneous leaps
stills.narration: No pair may have parallel fifths or octaves, or contrary fifths or octaves. Remember that contrary fifths are allowed when they are not between the soprano and the bass. And two simultaneous leaps in the same direction are not allowed, unless both are perfect fourths.

stills.heading: New rule: the leading tone in the soprano
stills.caption: It rises to the tonic · exception: III – IV
stills.narration: And there is a new rule for the leading tone. If the leading tone is in the soprano, and the next chord contains the tonic, the leading tone always rises to the tonic. The only exception is the connection from the third to the fourth degree.

stills.heading: The eight connections in the assignment
stills.caption: Each one in a different key
stills.narration: Now let's look at the eight connections in the assignment, each one in a different key.

stills.heading: 1 · I – IV in G major
stills.narration: First, from the first to the fourth degree, in G major.

stills.heading: 1 · I – IV in G major
stills.caption: G stays in the alto
stills.narration: G is the common tone, and it stays in the alto. The soprano rises from B to C, the tenor rises from D to E, and the bass goes down from G to C.

stills.heading: 2 · IV – V in D major
stills.narration: Second, from the fourth to the fifth degree, in D major.

stills.heading: 2 · IV – V in D major
stills.caption: No common tones: upper voices against the bass
stills.narration: These two chords have no common tones. So the bass rises by step, from G to A, and the other three voices go down to the nearest note. That way we avoid parallel fifths and octaves.

stills.heading: 3 · V – I in F major
stills.narration: Third, from the fifth to the first degree, in F major.

stills.heading: 3 · V – I in F major
stills.caption: The leading tone rises to the tonic
stills.narration: The leading tone, E, is in the soprano, and it rises to the tonic, F. C is the common tone and stays in the tenor, the alto rises from G to A, and the bass goes down from C to F.

stills.heading: 4 · II – V in B♭ major
stills.narration: Fourth, from the second to the fifth degree, in B flat major.

stills.heading: 4 · II – V in B♭ major
stills.caption: C stays in the soprano
stills.narration: C is the common tone and stays in the soprano. The alto rises from G to A, the tenor rises from E flat to F, and the bass goes down from C to F.

stills.heading: 5 · V – VI in A major
stills.narration: Fifth, from the fifth to the sixth degree, in A major.

stills.heading: 5 · V – VI in A major
stills.caption: The leading tone rises · in VI the third is doubled
stills.narration: The leading tone, G sharp, is in the soprano, and since the sixth degree contains the tonic, it rises to A. The bass rises from E to F sharp, and the alto and tenor go down. In the sixth degree we double the third, A, which is also the tonic.

stills.heading: 6 · VI – II in E♭ major
stills.narration: Sixth, from the sixth to the second degree, in E flat major.

stills.heading: 6 · VI – II in E♭ major
stills.caption: C stays in the tenor
stills.narration: C is the common tone and stays in the tenor. The soprano rises from G to A flat, the alto rises from E flat to F, and the bass goes down from C to F.

stills.heading: 7 · I – VII 6/3 in C major
stills.narration: Seventh, from the first degree to the seventh in six three, in C major.

stills.heading: 7 · I – VII 6/3 in C major
stills.caption: VII complete · D doubled · the leading tone only once
stills.narration: The bass rises from C to D, which is the third of the seventh degree. The soprano goes down from C to B, the alto goes down from G to F, and the tenor goes down from E to D. The seventh degree is complete, with D doubled, and the leading tone appears only once.

stills.heading: 8 · IV 6/3 – V in E major
stills.narration: Eighth, from the fourth degree in six three to the fifth, in E major.

stills.heading: 8 · IV 6/3 – V in E major
stills.caption: The bass moves down by step
stills.narration: The bass goes down from C sharp to B, by step. The soprano rises from A to B, the alto goes down from E to D sharp, and the tenor goes down from A to F sharp.

stills.heading: Two typical mistakes
stills.narration: Now let's look at two typical mistakes.

stills.heading: IV – V with every voice moving up
stills.caption: Parallel 5ths soprano–bass · parallel octaves tenor–bass
stills.narration: Here we connect the fourth and fifth degrees in C major, moving all the voices up. Between the soprano and the bass there are parallel fifths, and between the tenor and the bass there are parallel octaves.

stills.heading: Corrected
stills.caption: Upper voices in contrary motion to the bass
stills.narration: The solution is to move the upper voices in contrary motion to the bass.

stills.heading: V – I: the leading tone goes down
stills.caption: B → G in the soprano
stills.narration: And here, from the fifth to the first degree, the leading tone is in the soprano and goes down from B to G.

stills.heading: Corrected
stills.caption: The leading tone rises to C
stills.narration: Since the first degree contains the tonic, the leading tone had to rise to C.

stills.heading: Assignment for the Virtual Teacher
stills.narration: Now, the assignment for the virtual teacher.

stills.heading: A different major key for each connection
stills.caption: You choose which ones
stills.narration: Write each connection in a different major key; you choose which ones.

stills.heading: Eight connections, in any order
stills.caption: I–IV · IV–V · V–I · II–V · V–VI · VI–II · I–VII 6/3 · IV 6/3–V
stills.narration: In Storm Sequencer, in SATB mode, write the eight connections we just saw, in any order you like. From the first to the fourth, from the fourth to the fifth, from the fifth to the first, from the second to the fifth, from the fifth to the sixth, from the sixth to the second, from the first to the seventh in six three, and from the fourth in six three to the fifth. Chords without figures are in root position.

stills.heading: One measure per connection
stills.caption: Two half notes · key signature at the start of each measure · 16 chords
stills.narration: Each connection takes one measure of four four, with two half notes in all four voices. At the start of each measure, write the key signature of its key. That makes sixteen chords in total.

stills.heading: Export the MIDI and upload it
stills.narration: Export the MIDI file and upload it.

stills.heading: The Virtual Teacher checks
stills.caption: Key and connection · chords · each voice · 5ths and octaves · simultaneous leaps · leading tone
stills.narration: The virtual teacher recognizes the key of each connection, and which connection it is. It checks how each chord is built, how each voice moves, the fifths and octaves, the simultaneous leaps, and the leading tone. It checks nothing between one connection and the next: each measure is a separate exercise. And if it finds a mistake, it explains what it is and in which connection.

stills.heading: Let's recap
stills.narration: Let's recap.

stills.heading: Harmonic material
stills.narration: The harmonic material tells us which chords we use and in which position. The third and sixth go in root position, the seventh in six three, and six four is not used freely.

stills.heading: General table of connections
stills.narration: The general table of connections tells us where each chord can go, and it has some required continuations.

stills.heading: When connecting
stills.narration: When connecting, we build each chord correctly, take care of each voice, and check the six pairs of voices. And the leading tone in the soprano rises to the tonic.

stills.heading: Next lesson
stills.caption: The minor mode and its special cases
stills.narration: In the next lesson we will look at the minor mode and its special cases.

stills.heading: Thank you
stills.caption: See you in lesson 9
stills.narration: Thank you for joining me. See you in lesson nine.
